passage: People think caring for a parent is only about love. It's also about schedules. My father got Parkinson's when I was twenty-four. Suddenly I was juggling my IT job, his doctor visits and his medicines. My sister Gargi lived in Delhi and felt guilty all the time. At first I did everything and got angry with her quietly. Then we had a proper call. 'Karthik, give me jobs I can do from here,' she said. She took over the paperwork and insurance claims from Delhi, and sent money for a part-time helper. I handled the hospital visits. We made a shared calendar. Some nights I'm still exhausted and sad watching him struggle with buttons. But we're a team now, and I'm not doing it alone.

qa.q: What part of the care did Gargi take over?
qa.a: She took over the paperwork and insurance claims from Delhi and sent money for a part-time helper.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel before the proper call with Gargi?
qa.a: Karthik felt overwhelmed and quietly angry with Gargi for not sharing the load.

qa.q: What helped Karthik manage the father's care?
qa.a: Dividing tasks with Gargi, hiring a helper and keeping a shared calendar.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi living far away?
qa.a: She feels guilty about not being there, so doing the paperwork gives her a real way to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult managing time, money and feelings while caring for an ageing parent with their sister.

passage: I'm Vidya, and I live across the landing from Ujjwal. His grandmother moved in with him last spring after a fall. He's twenty-five, works shifts at a bank, and now I see him most mornings carrying her tea to the balcony before running for his bus. Sometimes I hear him on the phone with relatives, voice raised: 'I can't do everything.' Once I found him sitting on the stairs, just staring. I asked if he was okay, and he said he was fine, but he wasn't. I offered to check on her during the day. He hesitated, then accepted. He started paying a nurse for a few hours on weekends too. Now he leaves a note on her door with the day's plan.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's grandmother move in with him?
qa.a: She moved in after a fall.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal sitting on the stairs, just staring, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was exhausted and overwhelmed, even though he said he was fine.

qa.q: How could neighbours support a young carer like Ujjwal?
qa.a: By offering specific help, like checking on the grandmother during the day, and not waiting to be asked.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Ujjwal's situation?
qa.a: Vidya sees that he's carrying a lot and pretending to be fine, and steps in with practical help.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young man struggle and adapt while caring for his grandmother.

passage:
First week: Ankita's mother started forgetting to take her medicines. Ankita moved back from the hostel and slept on the living room sofa. She missed two work deadlines and snapped at her brother Saurabh on the phone.

A month later: The doctor suggested memory checks. Ankita and Saurabh sat down with a list: who pays for what, who visits when, and what Ma could still do herself. Saurabh couldn't come often, so he took over the bills. Ankita cried for a while after that call, though she felt steadier too.

Three months later: Ankita had a pill box on the table and an alarm on Ma's phone. She had joined a carers' support group that met on Sundays. Ma still forgot things. But Ankita was sleeping again.

qa.q: Where did Ankita sleep after moving back?
qa.a: She slept on the living room sofa.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the first week, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and stressed; she missed deadlines and snapped at Saurabh.

qa.q: What helped Ankita most over the three months?
qa.a: Sharing tasks with Saurabh, simple routines like a pill box and alarm, and joining a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt living far away?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty for not being there, and taking on the bills let him help in a real way.

grounding: Shows a young woman, over months, managing time, money and emotions while caring for her ageing mother.

passage: Kishore puttar, sit with your Gurleen Aunty. You look like I did at twenty-five. My mother-in-law had a stroke the year after my wedding, and suddenly I was the one bathing her, feeding her, running to the chemist between my school job and home. I loved her, but some nights I sat in the bathroom and wanted to scream. Then I felt guilty for wanting to. What saved me was not strength. It was a family meeting. I made a list of every task and every cost and put it in front of my husband and his two brothers. They were shocked. One paid for a day attendant; the other came every Sunday so I could rest. Her doctor also told us about a caregivers' group that met in the gurudwara hall. Those women understood without my explaining. You can't carry Bapuji alone either, puttar. Make your list.

qa.q: What happened to Gurleen's mother-in-law the year after her wedding?
qa.a: She had a stroke.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Gurleen have on hard nights?
qa.a: She loved her mother-in-law but felt like screaming, and then felt guilty for wanting to.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen share the load?
qa.a: A written list of every task and cost shown at a family meeting, which brought paid help and Sunday rest, plus a caregivers' group.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's husband and his brothers have felt seeing the list?
qa.a: Shocked, realising how much she had been carrying without them noticing.

grounding: An elder recalls managing the time, money and feelings of caring for an ailing relative by sharing the load.

passage: The day attendant didn't come, the monsoon had knocked out the lift, and Himani had a client call at eleven. Her father, whose memory had been slipping for two years, kept asking where her mother was; she had died three years ago. Each time Himani answered gently, 'She's not here, Papa. I'm here.' At 10:50 she called her sister Pallavi in Bhopal. 'I can't do this call and watch him.' Pallavi, who usually sent money rather than time, said, 'Put me on video with him. I'll talk to him for an hour.' Papa loved it. Himani took the call from the balcony, hair unwashed, voice steady. Afterwards she sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from tiredness. That evening the sisters made a plan: Pallavi would take two video hours a week and visit every month, and they would look for a backup attendant.

qa.q: What time was Himani's client call?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How did Himani feel after the call, and why?
qa.a: She sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from exhaustion after juggling work and her father's care alone.

qa.q: What did the sisters change so that care is shared more fairly?
qa.a: Pallavi will give two video hours a week and visit every month, and they will look for a backup attendant.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's role have felt different after that day?
qa.a: She moved from sending money to giving time, which may have made her feel closer to her father and sister.

grounding: Shows a young woman caring for her ageing father under pressure and sharing the load with her sister.
